For he does not say that I got money from them, or that I was induced by gifts to do this. But let us consider whether, wanting great things, I put off receiving favours from them until the time when they expected to rule, when I could have asked for great things and been granted greater ones. How, then, will this be made clear? Consider, O king, yourself and those who ruled still earlier than you — your brother, of course, and your father, and Nero — and [the times] in which they ruled; for it was chiefly under these emperors that I have lived in the public eye, spending the rest of my time visiting the Indians. In these thirty-eight years — for that is the length of time down to you — I have never gone to the doors of emperors, except to your father's in Egypt, since he was not yet emperor and acknowledged that he had come on my account; nor have I said anything servile to emperors, or to peoples about emperors; nor have I made a show of letters, whether from emperors writing to me or by displaying that I wrote to them myself; nor have I ever flattered emperors for gifts and so been carried away from myself. If, at any rate, you were to ask me, thinking of rich and poor, in which of these two classes I enrol myself, I will say among the very richest; for to need nothing is to me Lydia and the whole of the Pactolus. How, then, could I have put off the gifts of men not yet emperors until the time when I thought they would rule, I who did not even accept those offered by you [and your house], whose rule I considered secure? Or how could I have contemplated changes of reign, when I made no use even of the established reigns to win honour? And indeed, what a philosopher gets by flattering the powerful is shown by the case of Euphrates. For what has he got from that source — why do I say money? No, there are springs of wealth for him; and he now holds forth at the bankers' tables, a huckster, a sub-huckster, a tax-farmer, a moneylender, becoming everything that is sold and everything that sells; he is forever stamped upon the doors of the powerful, and stands at them longer than the doorkeepers, and has often been caught by the doorkeepers too, like the greedy among dogs; and though he has never parted with a drachma even to a philosopher, he fortifies his wealth as a base against others, feeding this Egyptian with money and sharpening against me a tongue that deserves to be cut out. Euphrates, then, I leave to you; for if you do not favour flatterers, you will find the fellow worse than I describe him; but hear the rest of my defence. What, then, is it, and about what? In the accusation, O king, a dirge was sung over an Arcadian boy: that he was cut open by me at night — whether he says in a dream, I do not yet know — and that this boy came of good parents and was in appearance like those Arcadians who are handsome in their squalor. They say that he was slaughtered as he begged and wept, and that I dipped my hands in the boy's blood and prayed to the gods to reveal the truth. Up to this point it is I they are trying; but the next part of the story touches the gods; for they say that the gods heard me when I prayed in this way, and gave favourable signs in the victim, and did not kill me for my impiety. As for how impure it is even to listen to such things, why should I speak of it, O king? But as for what I must defend: who is this Arcadian? For if he was not nameless as to his parentage, nor slavish in appearance, it is time for you to ask what was the name of those who begot him, of what house he was, what city in Arcadia reared him, and from what altars he was carried off to be sacrificed here. He does not say these things, though he is clever at not telling the truth. So it is over a slave that he puts me on trial. For one who has no name of his own, nor of those he was born from, who has no city, no inherited land — must he not, O gods, be ranked among slaves? For everything about him is nameless. Who, then, was the dealer in this slave? Who bought him from the Arcadians? For if the race of these people is suited to divination by slaughter, the boy was probably bought for a great deal of money, and someone must have sailed to the Peloponnese so that the Arcadian might be brought here to us from there; for slaves from Pontus or Lydia or Phrygia one could buy here too, since one may even meet whole droves of them coming here together; for these nations, and all those of the barbarians, having obeyed others all the time, do not yet think slavery shameful. Among the Phrygians, at any rate, it is a native custom even to sell their own people, and to give no further thought to them once enslaved. But the Greeks are still lovers of freedom, and a Greek will not sell even a slave beyond the borders; for this reason neither kidnappers nor slave-dealers can get access to them, and to Arcadia even less; for besides being more devoted to freedom than all the other Greeks, they also need a great crowd of slaves. For Arcadia is a land of many cornfields [and grassy], and wooded not only on the heights but in all the lower ground as well. So they need many farmers, and many goatherds and swineherds and shepherds, and herdsmen, some for cattle and some for horses; and the country needs many woodcutters, and they are trained for this from boyhood. But even if the situation of the Arcadians were not like this, and they could, like others, sell off their own slaves, what would the victim's coming from Arcadia contribute to this much-talked-of wisdom? For the Arcadians are not the wisest of the Greeks, that they should show anything more than any other man in the rational parts of their entrails; on the contrary, they are the most boorish of men, and swinish, in other respects and in gorging themselves on acorns. I have perhaps made my defence more rhetorically than is my manner, explaining the customs of the Arcadians and wandering off to the Peloponnese in my speech. For what is the defence proper to me? I did not sacrifice, I do not sacrifice, I do not touch blood, not even if it be blood on an altar; for so Pythagoras thought, and his followers likewise, and in Egypt the Naked Ones, and the wise men of the Indians, from whom the beginnings of wisdom came to Pythagoras and his school. Sacrificing in this way, they are not thought by the gods to do wrong; rather, the gods allow them to grow old with bodies sound and free of disease, and, ever wiser, to be thought subject to no tyrant and in need of nothing. And it is not unreasonable, I think, that they should ask for blessings in return for pure offerings. For I believe that the gods too, being of the same mind as I am about sacrifices, plant the frankincense-bearing regions of the earth in a pure part of the inhabited world, so that we may sacrifice from these without carrying iron in temples or sprinkling blood on altars. But I, it seems, forgetting myself and the gods, sacrificed in a manner that I am not accustomed to, and in which no human being would sacrifice. Let the occasion, too, which the accuser has named, acquit me of the charge; for on that day on which he says I did these things, if I was in the country, then I sacrificed; and if I sacrificed, then I also ate. Then you keep asking me, O king, whether I was not staying in Rome at that time? You too were living there, best of kings, but you would not say that you sacrificed such victims; and so was the informer, but he will not admit to doing what murderers do because he was living in Rome; and so were tens of thousands of people, whom it would be better to expel as aliens than to bring under indictments in which being here will be evidence of crimes. And yet coming to Rome perhaps even clears one of the charge of seeming to plot revolution; for living in a city in which everyone is eyes, and everyone is ears for what is and what is not, does not allow men to lay hands on revolution — those at least who are not too eager to die — and it makes the more cautious and prudent slow even to do what is permitted. What, then, informer, was I doing on that night? If you ask as you would ask yourself — since you too have come here to ask questions — I was preparing lawsuits and accusations against good men, and how to destroy the innocent, and how to persuade the emperor by telling him untruths, so that I might win credit and he be defiled. If you are inquiring as of a philosopher, I was praising the laughter of Democritus, which he laughs at all human affairs. But if you ask as of me, Philiscus the Malian, who had studied philosophy with me for four years, was ill at that time, and I was sleeping at his side, since he was in so bad a state that he actually died of the disease. And yet I would have prayed to have many *iynges* [magic charm-wheels] for his soul's sake, and, by Zeus, if there are any songs of Orpheus for the dead, not to be ignorant of those either; for I think I would even have gone beneath the earth for him, if such things were attainable; so closely had he bound me to himself by all that he did as a philosopher and in accordance with my own mind. You may hear this, O king, from Telesinus the consul too; for he also was at the Malian's side, tending him by night as much as I did. If you distrust Telesinus because he is one of those who practise philosophy, I call the doctors as witnesses; they are Seleucus of Cyzicus and Stratocles of Sidon. Ask them whether I speak the truth. And more than thirty pupils attended them, who are witnesses, of course, to the same things; for to summon here the relatives of Philiscus you would perhaps consider a postponement of the trial, since they set out from Rome at once for the homeland of the Malians, to perform the due rites for the dead man. Come forward, witnesses, for you have indeed been summoned for this purpose. WITNESSES. How far from the truth the indictment was composed, then, the testimony of these men shows clearly: [I was] not in the suburbs but in the city, not outside the walls but in a house, not at Nerva's but at Philiscus's, not slaughtering but praying for a life, not for empire but for philosophy, not electing a new man in your place but trying to save a man like myself. What, then, has the Arcadian to do with this? What of the tales of victims? What is the point of persuading [you] of such things? For even what has not happened will one day have happened, if it is judged as having happened. But the implausibility of the sacrifice, O king — where will you place that? There were indeed, in earlier times too, diviners by victims who were good at their art and worth naming — Megistias from Acarnania, Aristander from Lycia, and Ambracia produced Silanus — and they sacrificed, the Acarnanian for Leonidas, king of Sparta, the Lycian for Alexander the Macedonian, and Silanus for Cyrus when he coveted the kingship; and if anything clearer or wiser or truer had been stored away in a human being's entrails, the sacrifice would not have been hard to come by, with kings presiding over it, who had many cupbearers and many captives, whose lawless acts went without risk, and who had no fear of accusation if they slaughtered anyone. But, I think, it occurred to these men, as it occurs to me now that I am in danger over such things, that it is likely that irrational animals, since they are slaughtered in ignorance of death, have none of their entrails clouded, because they do not understand what they are about to suffer; but how is it likely that a man, who always has in his soul some dread of death even when it is not yet upon him, should, when it is already present and before his eyes, show anything prophetic in his entrails, or anything at all favourable to the sacrifice? That my conjecture about these things is right and in accordance with nature, consider, O king, as follows. The liver, in which those skilled in these matters say lies the tripod of their divination, is not composed of pure blood; for all the blood that is unmixed the heart keeps, channelling it through the blood-bearing veins into the whole body; while the bile, which lies upon the liver, is stirred up by anger, and drawn down by fears into the hollows of the liver. Seething under the things that provoke it, and no longer containable even in its own vessel, it pours out over the liver lying beneath, whereupon the bile entirely covers the smooth and prophetic parts of the organ; but under the things that frighten, it sinks down and draws with it the light in the smooth parts as well; for then the pure part of the blood also retreats, by which the liver becomes like a spleen, since by nature it runs beneath the membrane around the liver and floats upon the muddy part. What use, then, O king, is the bloodshed, if the victims are to give no signs? And human nature makes them signless, being aware of death, and so do the dying themselves; for the brave die in anger and the faint-hearted in fear. That is why the art, among those barbarians who are not without knowledge of it, recommends slaughtering she-goats and lambs, since these creatures are simple and not far from insensible, but cocks and pigs and bulls, since they are high-spirited, it does not admit to its secrets. I see, O king, that I am provoking the accuser, since I have made you a wiser listener, and you seem to me to be attending to my argument; and if I express any part of it unclearly, I give you leave to question me. I have said what I have to say in answer to the Egyptian's indictment; but since, I think, the slanders of Euphrates should not be overlooked either, may you, O king, judge which of us two is more truly a philosopher. Well, then: he strives to say what is untrue about me, but I do not think fit [to do so about him]; he considers you a master, I a ruler; he hands you a sword against me, I a reasoned word. But what he has slandered me over is the discourses which I delivered in Ionia, and he says that they were spoken by me against your interest. And yet what I said was about the Fates and necessity, and the affairs of kings served me as an example for my argument, since your affairs are thought the greatest of human things; and I discoursed on the power of the Fates, and on how what they spin is so unalterable that, if they were to vote the kingship to someone when it belonged to another, and that other were to kill him so that his rule might never be taken from him by this man, the dead man would come to life again to fulfil what the Fates had decided. For we bring exaggerations into our arguments because of those who are not persuaded by plausible ones, just as if I were to say something like this: "He who is destined to become a carpenter will be a carpenter, even if he has both hands cut off; and he who is destined to win the footrace at Olympia will not miss the victory, not even if he is lamed in the leg; and he to whom the Fates have granted mastery in archery will not miss the mark, not even if he loses his sight." And what I said about kings I said with an eye, of course, to men like Acrisius and Laius, and Astyages the Mede, and many others who seemed at the outset to be arranging their affairs well, of whom some thought they were killing their children, others their grandsons, and were robbed of their kingdoms by them, when these sprang up out of obscurity together with what was fated. And if I were fond of flattery, I would say that I had your case in mind too, when you were trapped here by Vitellius, and the temple of Zeus was burning on the brow of the city, and he declared that his own position would be secure if you did not escape him — and yet you were then quite a youth, and not yet what you are now; but nevertheless, since the Fates had decided otherwise, he perished, plans and all, and you now hold what was his. But since I dislike the mode of flattery — for it seems to me one of those that are out of rhythm and harsh to the ear — let this string be cut, and do not suppose that I had any of your affairs in mind, but that I discoursed only on the Fates and necessity; for this is what he says I said against you. And yet most of the gods put up with this doctrine, and not even Zeus is vexed when he hears the poets, in the Lycian episode, singing "Alas for me, that Sarpedon…" and such things about him, in which he says that he gives up his son to the Fates; and again saying, in the *Weighing of Souls*, that he honoured Minos, the brother of Sarpedon, when he had died, with a golden sceptre and appointed him to judge in the court of Aidoneus, but did not beg him off from the Fates. Why, then, O king, are you vexed at this doctrine, when the gods endure it — the gods, whose state is fixed for ever — and do not kill the poets for it? For it is fitting to follow the Fates and not to be harsh about changes of fortune, and not to disbelieve Sophocles — "To the gods alone comes no old age, nor ever death; all else all-mastering time confounds" — who spoke best of all men. For human good fortune goes round in a circle, and the span of happiness, O king, lasts but a day: this man has what was mine, and another what was his, and so-and-so, holding what was so-and-so's, does not hold it. Bearing this in mind, O king, put an end to exiles, put an end to bloodshed, and deal with philosophy as you please, for true philosophy at least cannot be harmed; but take away the tears of men; for as things are, a boundless echo comes from the sea, and a far greater one from the mainlands, of people lamenting whatever each has to lament. And the evils that spring from this, too many to be counted, are to be laid to the tongues of the informers, who slander everyone to you, and you, O king, to everyone.

fixed.before: The contest, O king, is over great matters, both for you and for me. For you are in danger over things no emperor ever was: of seeming to have been set against philosophy without any just cause; and I over things that not even Socrates once was at Athens, whom those who brought the indictment held to be an innovator in matters divine, but neither called nor thought a divinity. Since so grave a danger has come upon each of us, I will not hesitate to advise you, too, of what I have persuaded myself. For when the accuser brought us into this trial, an untrue opinion about me and about you entered the minds of the many: they thought that you would take anger as your counsellor in the hearing, and through it would even put me to death — whatever putting to death may be — and that I would remove myself from the court by one of the ways there are of running away; and there were, O king, ten thousand of them. Hearing this, I did not proceed to condemn you in advance, nor did I vote against your hearing as though it would not be straight; instead, having bound myself to the laws, I stand here to answer the charge. And this is the advice I give to you as well. For it is just not to condemn in advance, nor to sit already persuaded that I have done you some harm; nor, when you hear about the Armenian and the Babylonian and all who rule in those parts — who have cavalry beyond counting, and every kind of archery, and a land of gold, and a host of men, as I know — that you will suffer something at their hands which will rob you even of this empire, to hear it with a laugh, and yet to believe of a wise and naked man that he has a weapon against the emperor of the Romans, and to accept this when an Egyptian informer says it — things you never heard even from Athena, who you say watches over you. Unless, by Zeus, flattery and informing have now advanced so far among these accursed wretches that they claim the gods are fit counsellors for you in small matters — such things as inflamed eyes, or not catching a fever, or not having one of your organs swell up — touching you like doctors and treating whichever of these you are suffering from; but that when you are in danger in your empire and in your person, they do not come to advise you whom you must guard against, nor to teach you what weapon you will have against them; and that the informers are your aegis of Athena and your hand of Zeus, claiming to know on your behalf what not even the gods know, staying awake ahead of you and going to sleep ahead of you — if indeed these men ever sleep — pouring, as they say, evils upon evils, and forever composing these Iliads of theirs. As for their keeping horses and being rolled into the forum behind teams of white horses, and their gourmandising off silver and gold, and their marriages costing twenty thousand, and their favourite boys bought for thirty thousand, and their committing adultery for as long as they escape notice and then marrying the women they seduced once they are caught with them, and those who applaud them for their glorious victories whenever some philosopher or consul who has done no wrong is caught by them and put to death by you — let all this be conceded to the luxury of these accursed men, and to their no longer having any fear either of laws or of eyes; but to think so far above humankind as to wish to know things before the gods do — this I do not commend, and I am afraid even to hear of it; and if you were to accept it, they will perhaps indict you too, for discrediting belief in the divine; for one must expect that such indictments will be drawn up against you as well, once there is nobody left for the informers. I am aware that I am rebuking rather than defending myself; but let these things be said by me on behalf of the laws, for unless you consider them your rulers, you will not rule. Who, then, will be my advocate as I make my defence? For if I were to call on Zeus, under whom I know I have lived my life, they will say that I am practising sorcery and bringing heaven down to earth. Let us then discuss this matter with a man whom most people say is dead, though I say he is not. This is your father, to whom I am worth as much as he is to you; for he made you, but he was made by me. He, O king, will be my helper in this defence, knowing my affairs far better than you do. For he came to Egypt when he was not yet emperor, to sacrifice to the gods of Egypt and to consult me about the empire. And when he met me, with my long hair and dressed as I am now, he did not ask a single thing about my appearance, since he considered everything about me to be in good order; and admitting that he had come on my account, he went away praising me, having said to me what he said to no one else, and heard from me what he heard from no one else. And the resolve with which he set about ruling was strengthened in him chiefly by me, when it had already been shaken by others — men not ill-meaning, though not so in your view; for those who were persuading him not to rule were surely also robbing you of holding this power after him. But when I advised him not to think himself unworthy of an empire that was coming to his doors, and to make you [and your brother] its heirs, he said my advice was good, and he was himself raised to greatness and raised you with him. Had he thought me a sorcerer, he would not have made me a partner in his concerns. For he did not come and say things like this: "Compel the Fates, or Zeus, to declare me sole ruler," or "Work portents for me with signs from Zeus, showing the sun rising in the west and setting where it begins." For he would not have seemed to me fit to rule, either if he thought me capable of these things, or if he were hunting by tricks for an empire which ought to be won by virtues. Moreover, I conversed with him in public, in a temple; but the gatherings of sorcerers shun the temples of the gods, for these are hateful to those who practise that craft, and screening themselves with night and with everything lightless, they do not allow their foolish dupes to have either eyes or ears. He did talk with me in private too, but Euphrates and Dio were present all the same, the one most hostile to me, the other most friendly — for may I never cease to count Dio among my friends. Who, then, in the presence of wise men, or of men at least laying claim to wisdom, would engage in the talk of sorcerers? And who would not guard alike, among friends and among enemies, against appearing wicked? And the conversation itself was opposed to sorcerers. You, perhaps, think that your father, being in love with kingship, trusted sorcerers rather than himself, and got from me a means of compelling the gods so as to obtain it; but he believed he had that even before he came to Egypt, and afterwards he talked with me about greater things — about laws, and about just wealth — and he was eager to learn how the gods should be served, and what blessings come from them to those who rule according to the laws. Sorcerers are something opposed to all these things; for if these were to prevail, their craft will be nothing. It is fitting, O king, to have considered this as well. All the arts that exist among men accomplish different things, but all of them work for money — some for small sums, others for large, others for enough to live on — and not only the manual crafts, but of the other arts too, the wise and the half-wise alike, all except true philosophy. By wise arts I mean poetry, music, astronomy, the sophists, and those orators who are not of the marketplace; by half-wise, painting, modelling, sculptors, ship-pilots, and farmers, if they follow the seasons; for these arts too fall not far short of wisdom. There is [also] something, O king — false-sages and begging impostors — which you must not take to be divination; for divination is worth much, if it tells the truth, though whether it is an art I do not yet know; but it is sorcerers I call false-sages. For that what is not should be thought to be, and that what is should be disbelieved — all this I put down to the opinion of those who are deceived; for the cleverness of the craft rests on the folly of those who are deceived and who offer sacrifice. And the craft — they are all lovers of money; for the tricks they pride themselves on were devised by them for pay, and they hunt for excessive sums, luring those who desire anything whatever with the claim that they can do everything. What wealth, then, O king, have you seen about me, that you think I practise false wisdom — and that when your father considered me above money? And that I am telling the truth — where is that letter of mine from the noble and godlike man, in which he sings my praises for other things and for my poverty? "The emperor Vespasian to Apollonius the philosopher, greetings. If all men, Apollonius, were willing to practise philosophy in the same way as you, philosophy and poverty would both fare very happily: philosophy because it is incorruptible, and poverty because it is voluntary. Farewell." Let your father make this defence on my behalf, defining for me the incorruptibility of my philosophy and the voluntariness of my poverty; for he remembered, I suppose, what happened in Egypt, when Euphrates and many of those who pretend to philosophy came up to him and asked for money, not even covertly, while I not only did not approach him for money, but even pushed those men away as unsound. I had been set against money while I was still a youth: at any rate my father's property — and it was a splendid estate — I looked upon for one single day, and then gave it up to my brothers and my friends and to the poor among my relatives, practising, starting as it were from the hearth, to need nothing. Let me pass over Babylon, and the lands of the Indians beyond the Caucasus and the river Hyphasis, through which I travelled still true to myself; but of my conduct here, and of my not looking to silver, I call this Egyptian as witness. For though he says that I have done and plotted terrible things, he has not said for how much money I worked this mischief, nor what gain I had in view; but he thinks me such a fool as to practise sorcery, and to do without even being paid the wrongs that others do for large sums of money — proclaiming, I suppose, a market like this: "Come, you fools, for I practise sorcery, and not for money but for nothing; and you will profit by each going away with what he desires, and I by dangers and indictments." But so that we do not stray into foolish talk, let us ask the accuser which charge I should speak to first. And yet why need I ask? For he went through my dress at the beginning of his speech, and, by Zeus, through what I eat and do not eat. Defend yourself, then, on these points, divine Pythagoras; for we are on trial for practices which you discovered and I commend. The earth, O king, produces everything for men, and those who wish to keep a truce with the animals need nothing more; for some things they pluck from her, and others they reap by ploughing her as she nurses her young, as suits the seasons; but others, as if they had not heard the earth, have whetted the knife against the animals for the sake of clothing and food. Now the Indian Brahmans did not themselves approve of this, and they taught the Naked Ones of Egypt not to approve of it; and Pythagoras took it from there — he was the first of the Greeks to associate with the Egyptians — and he left living creatures to the earth, and ate what the earth itself produces, saying that it was undefiled, being fit to nourish both body and mind; and saying that the clothing which most men wear, made from dead animals, was not clean, he dressed himself in linen, and on the same principle wove his shoes of papyrus; and he reaped many benefits from his purity, but first of all that of perceiving his own soul. For he had been born in the times when Troy fought for Helen, and being the most beautiful of the sons of Panthous and the most beautifully dressed, he died so young as to give Homer occasion for a lament; and passing into several bodies according to the ordinance of Adrasteia, by which the soul changes [from body to body], he came back again into human form and was born to Mnesarchides of Samos, a sage instead of a barbarian, an Ionian instead of a Trojan, and so far undying that he had not even forgotten that he had been Euphorbus. I have told you, then, the ancestor of my wisdom, and that I did not discover these things myself, but hold them as heir of another. And I do not put on trial those who indulge themselves in the scarlet bird, or in the bird from the Phasis or from Paeonia, which those who gratify their bellies in everything fatten for their feasts; nor have I ever yet indicted anyone over the fish which the grandees buy for more than men once paid for koppa-branded horses; nor have I begrudged anyone a purple robe, or some Pamphylian or soft garment; yet I — O gods! — am defending myself against an indictment over asphodel and dried fruits and clean fare; and not even my clothing is safe from seizure, but the accuser strips me of that too, as something of great value to sorcerers. And yet, if you set aside the argument about living and lifeless things, by which a man is thought pure or not, in what way is linen better than wool? Wool was shorn from the gentlest of animals, one cherished by the gods, who do not disdain the shepherd's work, and who, by Zeus, once even deemed it worthy of a golden form — whether the gods did so or the stories. Flax is sown just anyhow, and there is no story of gold attached to it; but nevertheless, because it was not plucked from a living creature, it is thought pure by the Indians and pure by the Egyptians, and for this reason it has become the dress of Pythagoras and of me when we converse, pray, and sacrifice. It is pure, too, to spend the night under it; for to those who live as I do, dreams bring truer messages. Let us make a defence also for the hair I once had, since an indictment has been found even for squalor. Let the judge of it be not the Egyptian but the blond and well-combed youths, who have their lovers and the courtesans at whose doors they go revelling hanging upon them; and let them consider themselves fortunate and enviable for their hair and the perfume that drips from it, and me as utterly without charm, a lover of not loving. For this shall be said to them: "Wretches, do not slander the invention of the Dorians; for wearing long hair comes from the Lacedaemonians, who practised it in [the] times when they were at their most warlike; and Leonidas, king of Sparta, wore his hair long for the sake of courage, and to appear majestic to his friends and fearsome to his enemies; and that is why Sparta wears its hair long in pride of him, no less than of Lycurgus and Iphitus." Let iron spare a wise man's hair; for it is not right to bring it against the place where all the springs of the senses are, and all voices, whence prayers come forth, and speech, the interpreter of wisdom. Empedocles, indeed, even fitted a band of the deepest purple about his hair and strutted through the streets of the Greeks composing hymns to say that he would become a god instead of a man; while I, who wore my hair untended and never needed hymns of that kind about it, am dragged into indictments and law courts. And what am I to say of Empedocles? Was he singing of himself, or of the happiness of the men of his day, among whom such things were not made matter for informers? Let us say no more about my hair; for it has been cut off, and envy has forestalled the accusation — envy, on whose account I must defend myself on the other charge, which is a grave one, and of a kind, O king, to cause fear not only to you but to Zeus as well. For he says that men consider me a god and proclaim this publicly, being thunderstruck by me. And yet, before bringing the charge, he ought to have shown this: by what discourse, by what so wonderful a thing said or done, I induced men to pray to me. For I never discoursed among the Greeks on what my soul has changed from or into, or will change into — though I know it — nor did I send out such notions about myself, nor did I break forth into oracles and chanted prophecies, after the frenzied manner of those who call upon the gods; nor do I know of any city in which it was resolved to assemble and sacrifice to Apollonius. And yet I was of great value to each people in whatever they needed from me; and what they needed was such things as these: for the sick, not to be sick; to be initiated more piously, to sacrifice more piously, to have insolence cut out, to have the laws strengthened. My pay for these things was that they should show themselves better than they had been; and I was doing them as a favour to you. For just as those in charge of cattle oblige the owners of the cattle by keeping them from straying, and those who tend flocks fatten them for the profit of their owners, and bee-keepers rid the bees of their diseases so that the swarm may not be lost to its master, so too, I suppose, by putting a stop to the failings of civic life I was setting the cities right for you; so that even if they did think me a god, the deception brought profit to you; for they listened to me eagerly, afraid to do what a god does not approve. But that was not what they thought; they thought that there is a kinship between man and god, through which alone of living creatures he knows the gods, and reflects both on his own nature and on how he shares in the divine. So man declares that even his very form resembles a god, as sculpture and painting express it, and he is persuaded that the virtues come to him from god, and that those who share in them are near to the gods and godlike. As teachers of this way of thinking let us not call on the Athenians, even though they were the first to bestow titles like "the Just" and "the Olympian" and the like — titles too divine, probably, to be fitly given to a man — but on Apollo at Pytho. For Lycurgus of Sparta came to his temple when he had just drawn up the laws by which Lacedaemon is ordered, and Apollo, addressing him, weighs the opinion to be held of him: at the beginning of the oracle he says he is at a loss whether he should call him god or man, and as it proceeds he declares him worthy of this title and votes it to him, as a good man. And no trial or danger [came] upon Lycurgus from this among the Lacedaemonians, on the ground that he was making himself immortal because he did not rebuke the Pythian god when addressed in these terms; rather, they agreed with the oracle, having been persuaded of this, no doubt, even before it was given. As for the Indians and the Egyptians, the case is this. The Egyptians carp at the Indians in other respects and disparage their opinions on practical matters; but the doctrine that has been set out about the creator of the universe they praise so highly that they have even taught it to others, though it is the Indians'. The doctrine recognises god as the creator of the coming-to-be and of the being of the universe, and the reason he conceived these things as his being good. Since, then, these things are akin, I hold to this doctrine and say that good men have something of god in them. Let the *kosmos* [ordered world] that depends on god the creator be understood as all that is in heaven and in the sea and on earth, in which men have an equal share, save for fortune. But there is also a kind of order that depends on a good man, not exceeding the measures of wisdom, which you yourself, O king, will surely say requires a man made in the likeness of a god. And what is the shape of this order? Souls in disorder clutch at every fashion like madmen; laws are stale to them, self-control is nowhere, the honours of the gods are held in no honour, and they love chatter and luxury, from which springs idleness, a bad counsellor for every deed. Drunken souls leap at many things, and nothing curbs this skittishness, not even if they were to drink every potion that, like mandrake, is held to bring sleep. But there is need of a man who will take care of the order of these souls, a god come by way of wisdom. For such a man is able to lead them away from the passions to which they are carried off more savagely than in ordinary intercourse, and from the love of money, on account of which they say they do not yet have everything, so long as they are not also holding their mouths open beneath the wealth pouring in upon them. For to restrain them from laying hands on murder is perhaps not impossible for such a man; but to wash murder away is possible neither for me nor for god, the creator of all things. Let there be an accusation, O king, over Ephesus too, since it was saved; and let the Egyptian prosecute me in the way that suits his indictment. For the accusation, I suppose, runs like this: "Among the Scythians or the Celts who live along the river Ister or the Rhine, a city has been founded no smaller than Ephesus in Ionia; this city, which is a base for barbarians who do not obey you, a plague was about to destroy, but Apollonius cured it." Even to this a wise man has a defence, if the king wishes to overcome what opposes him by arms and not by diseases; for may no city be wiped out, either for your sake, O king, or for mine, and may I never see disease at the temples, so that the sick shall lie in them. But let the affairs of barbarians not be our concern, nor let us enrol them among the healthy, since they are most hostile to us and not at truce with our race. But who will deny Ephesus its salvation — Ephesus, which took the first beginnings of its race from the purest Attica, which has grown greater than all the cities of Ionia and Lydia, which has advanced out to the sea because it outgrew the land on which it was founded, and which is full of the studies of philosophers and orators, through which the city is strong not in horses but in its tens of thousands of people, because it honours wisdom? And what wise man do you think would shrink from the struggle for such a city, when he called to mind Democritus, who once freed the people of Abdera from a plague, and thought of Sophocles the Athenian, who is said to have charmed the winds when they were blowing out of season, and had heard what Empedocles did, who held back the onrush of a cloud that had burst over the people of Acragas? The accuser interrupts me — you hear him too, O king, I suppose — and says that I am indicted not because I was the cause of the Ephesians' safety, but because I foretold that the disease would fall upon them; for this, he says, is beyond wisdom and something monstrous, and I could not have reached so great a degree of truth unless I were a sorcerer and a man of forbidden arts. What, then, will Socrates say here about the things he claimed to learn from his divine sign? And what will Thales and Anaxagoras say, the two Ionians, the one of whom foretold the plentiful crop of olives, and the other many events in the heavens? Did they foretell these things by sorcery? And yet these men were brought before courts on other charges, and nowhere among the charges is it said that they were sorcerers because they knew things beforehand. For this seemed ridiculous, and not plausible to say against wise men even in Thessaly, where the women had a bad name for drawing down the moon. How, then, did I perceive the calamity at Ephesus? You heard the accuser himself say that I do not live as others do, and I said at the outset about my own food that it is light and sweeter than other men's Sybaritic fare. This, O king, keeps my senses in a kind of ineffable clear air, and does not allow anything murky to hang about them, and lets them see through, as in the gleam of a mirror, everything that is happening and that is to be. For the wise man will not wait for the earth to send up its vapours, or for the air to be corrupted, if the harm flows from above; he will perceive these things even when they are at the door, later than the gods but sooner than the many; for gods perceive what is to come, men what is happening, and wise men what is approaching. Ask me about the causes of plagues in private, O king; for they are too wise to be spoken of before the many. Does living in this way, then, produce only fineness of the senses, or also strength for the greatest and most wonderful deeds? What I mean may be seen from other cases too, but not least from what was done at Ephesus concerning that disease. For the form of the plague — it had taken the likeness of an old beggar — I both saw, and having seen it, I seized it, not stopping a disease but rooting it out; and to whom I prayed is shown by the shrine which I founded at Ephesus for this: it is a shrine of Heracles the Averter, and I chose him as my helper because, being wise and brave, he once cleansed Elis of plague by washing away the vapours which the land gave off when Augeas was its tyrant. Who, then, O king, do you think, if he were eager to appear a sorcerer, would dedicate to a god what he himself had accomplished? What admirers of his craft would he win, if he had handed over the admiration to a god? And who that was a sorcerer would pray to Heracles? For the wretches ascribe such things to pits and to the gods beneath the earth, from among whom Heracles must be set apart, for he is pure and kindly toward men. I prayed to him once in the Peloponnese too; for there also, around Corinth, a phantom of a *lamia* [a man-devouring spirit] was roaming about, feeding on the handsome young men; and he helped me in the contest, asking for no marvellous gifts, but a honey cake and frankincense and the chance to do something for the salvation of men; for in the days of Eurystheus too he considered this the reward of his labours. Do not be vexed, O king, at hearing about Heracles; for Athena cared for him, because he was good and a saviour to men. But since you bid me defend myself regarding the sacrifice — for you are pointing to it with your hand as well — hear a true defence. I, who do everything for the salvation of men, have never yet sacrificed on their behalf, nor would I sacrifice anything, nor touch offerings in which there is blood, nor pray with my eyes on a knife, or on a sacrifice such as he speaks of. It is no Scythian you have caught, O king, nor anyone from some land cut off from other men; nor have I ever mingled with the Massagetae or the Taurians — though if I had, I would have turned even them from their custom of sacrifice. To what a pitch of folly would I have driven, that I, who have discoursed so much about divination and about where it has force and where it does not, and who understand better than any man that the gods reveal their purposes to holy and wise men even when they do not practise divination, should lay hands on bloodshed, and on entrails which for me are unholy to offer and of ill omen? For such things even the voice of the divine would have abandoned me as impure. And indeed, if one were to set aside the abomination of the sacrifice and test the accuser against what he said a little earlier, he himself acquits me of the charge. For I, whom he says foretold the disease to the Ephesians without needing any sacrifice — why would I have needed victims for things I could know even without sacrificing? And why would I have needed divination about matters of which I myself was already convinced, and another man too? For if I am on trial over Nerva and those about him, I will say again what I said the other day when you brought this charge. I consider Nerva worthy of any office and of every word that tends to his praise, but no capable contender in weighty enterprises; for his body is broken down by illness, because of which his mind too is full of distress and not equal even to his household affairs. You, at any rate, he praises for your body and praises for your mind — doing, I think, what is natural; for human nature is in truth more eager to praise what it does not itself have strength in. Nerva also has a certain good feeling towards me; and I have never known him to laugh in my presence, or to indulge in any of the foolery that is usual among friends; but like youths before their own fathers and teachers, he speaks cautiously in all that he says in my presence, and still blushes; and knowing that I praise modesty, he cultivates it so excessively that he seems even to me humbler than is right. How, then, could anyone think it plausible that Nerva desired empire, when he is content if he can govern his own household? Or that he talked with me about great matters, when he has not had the courage to do so even about small ones? Or that he joined counsel with me on matters on which he would not have joined counsel even with anyone else, if he had my views in mind? Or how am I still wise at interpreting a man's mind, if I put my trust in divination but distrust wisdom? As for Orfitus and Rufus, just and temperate men, but sluggish, as I well know — if they say that these were accused as aspiring to tyranny, I do not know whether they are more wide of the mark about them or about Nerva; and if as having been his advisers, is Nerva more likely to have attempted to seize the empire, or these men to have advised it? Yet the man who judges these matters ought also to have considered this: what was I aiming at in helping men bent on revolution? For he does not say that I got money from them, or that I was induced by gifts to do this. But let us consider whether, wanting great things, I put off receiving favours from them until the time when they expected to rule, when I could have asked for great things and been granted greater ones. How, then, will this be made clear? Consider, O king, yourself and those who ruled still earlier than you — your brother, of course, and your father, and Nero — and [the times] in which they ruled; for it was chiefly under these emperors that I have lived in the public eye, spending the rest of my time visiting the Indians. In these thirty-eight years — for that is the length of time down to you — I have never gone to the doors of emperors, except to your father's in Egypt, since he was not yet emperor and acknowledged that he had come on my account; nor have I said anything servile to emperors, or to peoples about emperors; nor have I made a show of letters, whether from emperors writing to me or by displaying that I wrote to them myself; nor have I ever flattered emperors for gifts and so been carried away from myself. If, at any rate, you were to ask me, thinking of rich and poor, in which of these two classes I enrol myself, I will say among the very richest; for to need nothing is to me Lydia and the whole of the Pactolus. How, then, could I have put off the gifts of men not yet emperors until the time when I thought they would rule, I who did not even accept those offered by you [and your house], whose rule I considered secure? Or how could I have contemplated changes of reign, when I made no use even of the established reigns to win honour? And indeed, what a philosopher gets by flattering the powerful is shown by the case of Euphrates. For what has he got from that source — why do I say money? No, there are springs of wealth for him; and he now holds forth at the bankers' tables, a huckster, a sub-huckster, a tax-farmer, a moneylender, becoming everything that is sold and everything that sells; he is forever stamped upon the doors of the powerful, and stands at them longer than the doorkeepers, and has often been caught by the doorkeepers too, like the greedy among dogs; and though he has never parted with a drachma even to a philosopher, he fortifies his wealth as a base against others, feeding this Egyptian with money and sharpening against me a tongue that deserves to be cut out. Euphrates, then, I leave to you; for if you do not favour flatterers, you will find the fellow worse than I describe him; but hear the rest of my defence. What, then, is it, and about what? In the accusation, O king, a dirge was sung over an Arcadian boy: that he was cut open by me at night — whether he says in a dream, I do not yet know — and that this boy came of good parents and was in appearance like those Arcadians who are handsome in their squalor. They say that he was slaughtered as he begged and wept, and that I dipped my hands in the boy's blood and prayed to the gods to reveal the truth. Up to this point it is I they are trying; but the next part of the story touches the gods; for they say that the gods heard me when I prayed in this way, and gave favourable signs in the victim, and did not kill me for my impiety. As for how impure it is even to listen to such things, why should I speak of it, O king? But as for what I must defend: who is this Arcadian? For if he was not nameless as to his parentage, nor slavish in appearance, it is time for you to ask what was the name of those who begot him, of what house he was, what city in Arcadia reared him, and from what altars he was carried off to be sacrificed here. He does not say these things, though he is clever at not telling the truth. So it is over a slave that he puts me on trial. For one who has no name of his own, nor of those he was born from, who has no city, no inherited land — must he not, O gods, be ranked among slaves? For everything about him is nameless. Who, then, was the dealer in this slave? Who bought him from the Arcadians? For if the race of these people is suited to divination by slaughter, the boy was probably bought for a great deal of money, and someone must have sailed to the Peloponnese so that the Arcadian might be brought here to us from there; for slaves from Pontus or Lydia or Phrygia one could buy here too, since one may even meet whole droves of them coming here together; for these nations, and all those of the barbarians, having obeyed others all the time, do not yet think slavery shameful. Among the Phrygians, at any rate, it is a native custom even to sell their own people, and to give no further thought to them once enslaved. But the Greeks are still lovers of freedom, and a Greek will not sell even a slave beyond the borders; for this reason neither kidnappers nor slave-dealers can get access to them, and to Arcadia even less; for besides being more devoted to freedom than all the other Greeks, they also need a great crowd of slaves. For Arcadia is a land of many cornfields [and grassy], and wooded not only on the heights but in all the lower ground as well. So they need many farmers, and many goatherds and swineherds and shepherds, and herdsmen, some for cattle and some for horses; and the country needs many woodcutters, and they are trained for this from boyhood. But even if the situation of the Arcadians were not like this, and they could, like others, sell off their own slaves, what would the victim's coming from Arcadia contribute to this much-talked-of wisdom? For the Arcadians are not the wisest of the Greeks, that they should show anything more than any other man in the rational parts of their entrails; on the contrary, they are the most boorish of men, and swinish, in other respects and in gorging themselves on acorns. I have perhaps made my defence more rhetorically than is my manner, explaining the customs of the Arcadians and wandering off to the Peloponnese in my speech. For what is the defence proper to me? I did not sacrifice, I do not sacrifice, I do not touch blood, not even if it be blood on an altar; for so Pythagoras thought, and his followers likewise, and in Egypt the Naked Ones, and the wise men of the Indians, from whom the beginnings of wisdom came to Pythagoras and his school. Sacrificing in this way, they are not thought by the gods to do wrong; rather, the gods allow them to grow old with bodies sound and free of disease, and, ever wiser, to be thought subject to no tyrant and in need of nothing. And it is not unreasonable, I think, that they should ask for blessings in return for pure offerings. For I believe that the gods too, being of the same mind as I am about sacrifices, plant the frankincense-bearing regions of the earth in a pure part of the inhabited world, so that we may sacrifice from these without carrying iron in temples or sprinkling blood on altars. But I, it seems, forgetting myself and the gods, sacrificed in a manner that I am not accustomed to, and in which no human being would sacrifice. Let the occasion, too, which the accuser has named, acquit me of the charge; for on that day on which he says I did these things, if I was in the country, then I sacrificed; and if I sacrificed, then I also ate. Then you keep asking me, O king, whether I was not staying in Rome at that time? You too were living there, best of kings, but you would not say that you sacrificed such victims; and so was the informer, but he will not admit to doing what murderers do because he was living in Rome; and so were tens of thousands of people, whom it would be better to expel as aliens than to bring under indictments in which being here will be evidence of crimes. And yet coming to Rome perhaps even clears one of the charge of seeming to plot revolution; for living in a city in which everyone is eyes, and everyone is ears for what is and what is not, does not allow men to lay hands on revolution — those at least who are not too eager to die — and it makes the more cautious and prudent slow even to do what is permitted. What, then, informer, was I doing on that night? If you ask as you would ask yourself — since you too have come here to ask questions — I was preparing lawsuits and accusations against good men, and how to destroy the innocent, and how to persuade the emperor by telling him untruths, so that I might win credit and he be defiled. If you are inquiring as of a philosopher, I was praising the laughter of Democritus, which he laughs at all human affairs. But if you ask as of me, Philiscus the Malian, who had studied philosophy with me for four years, was ill at that time, and I was sleeping at his side, since he was in so bad a state that he actually died of the disease. And yet I would have prayed to have many *iynges* [magic charm-wheels] for his soul's sake, and, by Zeus, if there are any songs of Orpheus for the dead, not to be ignorant of those either; for I think I would even have gone beneath the earth for him, if such things were attainable; so closely had he bound me to himself by all that he did as a philosopher and in accordance with my own mind. You may hear this, O king, from Telesinus the consul too; for he also was at the Malian's side, tending him by night as much as I did. If you distrust Telesinus because he is one of those who practise philosophy, I call the doctors as witnesses; they are Seleucus of Cyzicus and Stratocles of Sidon. Ask them whether I speak the truth. And more than thirty pupils attended them, who are witnesses, of course, to the same things; for to summon here the relatives of Philiscus you would perhaps consider a postponement of the trial, since they set out from Rome at once for the homeland of the Malians, to perform the due rites for the dead man. Come forward, witnesses, for you have indeed been summoned for this purpose. WITNESSES. How far from the truth the indictment was composed, then, the testimony of these men shows clearly: [I was] not in the suburbs but in the city, not outside the walls but in a house, not at Nerva's but at Philiscus's, not slaughtering but praying for a life, not for empire but for philosophy, not electing a new man in your place but trying to save a man like myself. What, then, has the Arcadian to do with this? What of the tales of victims? What is the point of persuading [you] of such things? For even what has not happened will one day have happened, if it is judged as having happened. But the implausibility of the sacrifice, O king — where will you place that? There were indeed, in earlier times too, diviners by victims who were good at their art and worth naming — Megistias from Acarnania, Aristander from Lycia, and Ambracia produced Silanus — and they sacrificed, the Acarnanian for Leonidas, king of Sparta, the Lycian for Alexander the Macedonian, and Silanus for Cyrus when he coveted the kingship; and if anything clearer or wiser or truer had been stored away in a human being's entrails, the sacrifice would not have been hard to come by, with kings presiding over it, who had many cupbearers and many captives, whose lawless acts went without risk, and who had no fear of accusation if they slaughtered anyone. But, I think, it occurred to these men, as it occurs to me now that I am in danger over such things, that it is likely that irrational animals, since they are slaughtered in ignorance of death, have none of their entrails clouded, because they do not understand what they are about to suffer; but how is it likely that a man, who always has in his soul some dread of death even when it is not yet upon him, should, when it is already present and before his eyes, show anything prophetic in his entrails, or anything at all favourable to the sacrifice? That my conjecture about these things is right and in accordance with nature, consider, O king, as follows. The liver, in which those skilled in these matters say lies the tripod of their divination, is not composed of pure blood; for all the blood that is unmixed the heart keeps, channelling it through the blood-bearing veins into the whole body; while the bile, which lies upon the liver, is stirred up by anger, and drawn down by fears into the hollows of the liver. Seething under the things that provoke it, and no longer containable even in its own vessel, it pours out over the liver lying beneath, whereupon the bile entirely covers the smooth and prophetic parts of the organ; but under the things that frighten, it sinks down and draws with it the light in the smooth parts as well; for then the pure part of the blood also retreats, by which the liver becomes like a spleen, since by nature it runs beneath the membrane around the liver and floats upon the muddy part. What use, then, O king, is the bloodshed, if the victims are to give no signs? And human nature makes them signless, being aware of death, and so do the dying themselves; for the brave die in anger and the faint-hearted in fear. That is why the art, among those barbarians who are not without knowledge of it, recommends slaughtering she-goats and lambs, since these creatures are simple and not far from insensible, but cocks and pigs and bulls, since they are high-spirited, it does not admit to its secrets. I see, O king, that I am provoking the accuser, since I have made you a wiser listener, and you seem to me to be attending to my argument; and if I express any part of it unclearly, I give you leave to question me. I have said what I have to say in answer to the Egyptian's indictment; but since, I think, the slanders of Euphrates should not be overlooked either, may you, O king, judge which of us two is more truly a philosopher. Well, then: he strives to say what is untrue about me, but I do not think fit [to do so about him]; he considers you a master, I a ruler; he hands you a sword against me, I a reasoned word. But what he has slandered me over is the discourses which I delivered in Ionia, and he says that they were spoken by me against your interest. And yet what I said was about the Fates and necessity, and the affairs of kings served me as an example for my argument, since your affairs are thought the greatest of human things; and I discoursed on the power of the Fates, and on how what they spin is so unalterable that, if they were to vote the kingship to someone when it belonged to another, and that other were to kill him so that his rule might never be taken from him by this man, the dead man would come to life again to fulfil what the Fates had decided. For we bring exaggerations into our arguments because of those who are not persuaded by plausible ones, just as if I were to say something like this: "He who is destined to become a carpenter will be a carpenter, even if he has both hands cut off; and he who is destined to win the footrace at Olympia will not miss the victory, not even if he is lamed in the leg; and he to whom the Fates have granted mastery in archery will not miss the mark, not even if he loses his sight." And what I said about kings I said with an eye, of course, to men like Acrisius and Laius, and Astyages the Mede, and many others who seemed at the outset to be arranging their affairs well, of whom some thought they were killing their children, others their grandsons, and were robbed of their kingdoms by them, when these sprang up out of obscurity together with what was fated. And if I were fond of flattery, I would say that I had your case in mind too, when you were trapped here by Vitellius, and the temple of Zeus was burning on the brow of the city, and he declared that his own position would be secure if you did not escape him — and yet you were then quite a youth, and not yet what you are now; but nevertheless, since the Fates had decided otherwise, he perished, plans and all, and you now hold what was his. But since I dislike the mode of flattery — for it seems to me one of those that are out of rhythm and harsh to the ear — let this string be cut, and do not suppose that I had any of your affairs in mind, but that I discoursed only on the Fates and necessity; for this is what he says I said against you. And yet most of the gods put up with this doctrine, and not even Zeus is vexed when he hears the poets, in the Lycian episode, singing "Alas for me, that Sarpedon…" and such things about him, in which he says that he gives up his son to the Fates; and again saying, in the *Weighing of Souls*, that he honoured Minos, the brother of Sarpedon, when he had died, with a golden sceptre and appointed him to judge in the court of Aidoneus, but did not beg him off from the Fates. Why, then, O king, are you vexed at this doctrine, when the gods endure it — the gods, whose state is fixed for ever — and do not kill the poets for it? For it is fitting to follow the Fates and not to be harsh about changes of fortune, and not to disbelieve Sophocles — "To the gods alone comes no old age, nor ever death; all else all-mastering time confounds" — who spoke best of all men. For human good fortune goes round in a circle, and the span of happiness, O king, lasts but a day: this man has what was mine, and another what was his, and so-and-so, holding what was so-and-so's, does not hold it. Bearing this in mind, O king, put an end to exiles, put an end to bloodshed, and deal with philosophy as you please, for true philosophy at least cannot be harmed; but take away the tears of men; for as things are, a boundless echo comes from the sea, and a far greater one from the mainlands, of people lamenting whatever each has to lament. And the evils that spring from this, too many to be counted, are to be laid to the tongues of the informers, who slander everyone to you, and you, O king, to everyone.
fixed.after: The contest, O king, is over great matters, both for you and for me. For you are in danger over things no emperor ever was: of seeming to have been set against philosophy without any just cause; and I over things that not even Socrates once was at Athens, whom those who brought the indictment held to be an innovator in matters divine, but neither called nor thought a divinity. Since so grave a danger has come upon each of us, I will not hesitate to advise you, too, of what I have persuaded myself. For when the accuser brought us into this trial, an untrue opinion about me and about you entered the minds of the many: they thought that you would take anger as your counsellor in the hearing, and through it would even put me to death — whatever putting to death may be — and that I would remove myself from the court by one of the ways there are of running away; and there were, O king, ten thousand of them. Hearing this, I did not proceed to condemn you in advance, nor did I vote against your hearing as though it would not be straight; instead, having bound myself to the laws, I stand here to answer the charge. And this is the advice I give to you as well. For it is just not to condemn in advance, nor to sit already persuaded that I have done you some harm; nor, when you hear about the Armenian and the Babylonian and all who rule in those parts — who have cavalry beyond counting, and every kind of archery, and a land of gold, and a host of men, as I know — that you will suffer something at their hands which will rob you even of this empire, to hear it with a laugh, and yet to believe of a wise and naked man that he has a weapon against the emperor of the Romans, and to accept this when an Egyptian informer says it — things you never heard even from Athena, who you say watches over you. Unless, by Zeus, flattery and informing have now advanced so far among these accursed wretches that they claim the gods are fit counsellors for you in small matters — such things as inflamed eyes, or not catching a fever, or not having one of your organs swell up — touching you like doctors and treating whichever of these you are suffering from; but that when you are in danger in your empire and in your person, they do not come to advise you whom you must guard against, nor to teach you what weapon you will have against them; and that the informers are your aegis of Athena and your hand of Zeus, claiming to know on your behalf what not even the gods know, staying awake ahead of you and going to sleep ahead of you — if indeed these men ever sleep — pouring, as they say, evils upon evils, and forever composing these Iliads of theirs. As for their keeping horses and being rolled into the forum behind teams of white horses, and their gourmandising off silver and gold, and their marriages costing twenty thousand, and their favourite boys bought for thirty thousand, and their committing adultery for as long as they escape notice and then marrying the women they seduced once they are caught with them, and those who applaud them for their glorious victories whenever some philosopher or consul who has done no wrong is caught by them and put to death by you — let all this be conceded to the luxury of these accursed men, and to their no longer having any fear either of laws or of eyes; but to think so far above humankind as to wish to know things before the gods do — this I do not commend, and I am afraid even to hear of it; and if you were to accept it, they will perhaps indict you too, for discrediting belief in the divine; for one must expect that such indictments will be drawn up against you as well, once there is nobody left for the informers. I am aware that I am rebuking rather than defending myself; but let these things be said by me on behalf of the laws, for unless you consider them your rulers, you will not rule. Who, then, will be my advocate as I make my defence? For if I were to call on Zeus, under whom I know I have lived my life, they will say that I am practising sorcery and bringing heaven down to earth. Let us then discuss this matter with a man whom most people say is dead, though I say he is not. This is your father, to whom I am worth as much as he is to you; for he made you, but he was made by me. He, O king, will be my helper in this defence, knowing my affairs far better than you do. For he came to Egypt when he was not yet emperor, to sacrifice to the gods of Egypt and to consult me about the empire. And when he met me, with my long hair and dressed as I am now, he did not ask a single thing about my appearance, since he considered everything about me to be in good order; and admitting that he had come on my account, he went away praising me, having said to me what he said to no one else, and heard from me what he heard from no one else. And the resolve with which he set about ruling was strengthened in him chiefly by me, when it had already been shaken by others — men not ill-meaning, though not so in your view; for those who were persuading him not to rule were surely also robbing you of holding this power after him. But when I advised him not to think himself unworthy of an empire that was coming to his doors, and to make you [and your brother] its heirs, he said my advice was good, and he was himself raised to greatness and raised you with him. Had he thought me a sorcerer, he would not have made me a partner in his concerns. For he did not come and say things like this: "Compel the Fates, or Zeus, to declare me sole ruler," or "Work portents for me with signs from Zeus, showing the sun rising in the west and setting where it begins." For he would not have seemed to me fit to rule, either if he thought me capable of these things, or if he were hunting by tricks for an empire which ought to be won by virtues. Moreover, I conversed with him in public, in a temple; but the gatherings of sorcerers shun the temples of the gods, for these are hateful to those who practise that craft, and screening themselves with night and with everything lightless, they do not allow their foolish dupes to have either eyes or ears. He did talk with me in private too, but Euphrates and Dio were present all the same, the one most hostile to me, the other most friendly — for may I never cease to count Dio among my friends. Who, then, in the presence of wise men, or of men at least laying claim to wisdom, would engage in the talk of sorcerers? And who would not guard alike, among friends and among enemies, against appearing wicked? And the conversation itself was opposed to sorcerers. You, perhaps, think that your father, being in love with kingship, trusted sorcerers rather than himself, and got from me a means of compelling the gods so as to obtain it; but he believed he had that even before he came to Egypt, and afterwards he talked with me about greater things — about laws, and about just wealth — and he was eager to learn how the gods should be served, and what blessings come from them to those who rule according to the laws. Sorcerers are something opposed to all these things; for if these were to prevail, their craft will be nothing. It is fitting, O king, to have considered this as well. All the arts that exist among men accomplish different things, but all of them work for money — some for small sums, others for large, others for enough to live on — and not only the manual crafts, but of the other arts too, the wise and the half-wise alike, all except true philosophy. By wise arts I mean poetry, music, astronomy, the sophists, and those orators who are not of the marketplace; by half-wise, painting, modelling, sculptors, ship-pilots, and farmers, if they follow the seasons; for these arts too fall not far short of wisdom. There is [also] something, O king — false-sages and begging impostors — which you must not take to be divination; for divination is worth much, if it tells the truth, though whether it is an art I do not yet know; but it is sorcerers I call false-sages. For that what is not should be thought to be, and that what is should be disbelieved — all this I put down to the opinion of those who are deceived; for the cleverness of the craft rests on the folly of those who are deceived and who offer sacrifice. And the craft — they are all lovers of money; for the tricks they pride themselves on were devised by them for pay, and they hunt for excessive sums, luring those who desire anything whatever with the claim that they can do everything. What wealth, then, O king, have you seen about me, that you think I practise false wisdom — and that when your father considered me above money? And that I am telling the truth — where is that letter of mine from the noble and godlike man, in which he sings my praises for other things and for my poverty? "The emperor Vespasian to Apollonius the philosopher, greetings. If all men, Apollonius, were willing to practise philosophy in the same way as you, philosophy and poverty would both fare very happily: philosophy because it is incorruptible, and poverty because it is voluntary. Farewell." Let your father make this defence on my behalf, defining for me the incorruptibility of my philosophy and the voluntariness of my poverty; for he remembered, I suppose, what happened in Egypt, when Euphrates and many of those who pretend to philosophy came up to him and asked for money, not even covertly, while I not only did not approach him for money, but even pushed those men away as unsound. I had been set against money while I was still a youth: at any rate my father's property — and it was a splendid estate — I looked upon for one single day, and then gave it up to my brothers and my friends and to the poor among my relatives, practising, starting as it were from the hearth, to need nothing. Let me pass over Babylon, and the lands of the Indians beyond the Caucasus and the river Hyphasis, through which I travelled still true to myself; but of my conduct here, and of my not looking to silver, I call this Egyptian as witness. For though he says that I have done and plotted terrible things, he has not said for how much money I worked this mischief, nor what gain I had in view; but he thinks me such a fool as to practise sorcery, and to do without even being paid the wrongs that others do for large sums of money — proclaiming, I suppose, a market like this: "Come, you fools, for I practise sorcery, and not for money but for nothing; and you will profit by each going away with what he desires, and I by dangers and indictments." But so that we do not stray into foolish talk, let us ask the accuser which charge I should speak to first. And yet why need I ask? For he went through my dress at the beginning of his speech, and, by Zeus, through what I eat and do not eat. Defend yourself, then, on these points, divine Pythagoras; for we are on trial for practices which you discovered and I commend. The earth, O king, produces everything for men, and those who wish to keep a truce with the animals need nothing more; for some things they pluck from her, and others they reap by ploughing her as she nurses her young, as suits the seasons; but others, as if they had not heard the earth, have whetted the knife against the animals for the sake of clothing and food. Now the Indian Brahmans did not themselves approve of this, and they taught the Naked Ones of Egypt not to approve of it; and Pythagoras took it from there — he was the first of the Greeks to associate with the Egyptians — and he left living creatures to the earth, and ate what the earth itself produces, saying that it was undefiled, being fit to nourish both body and mind; and saying that the clothing which most men wear, made from dead animals, was not clean, he dressed himself in linen, and on the same principle wove his shoes of papyrus; and he reaped many benefits from his purity, but first of all that of perceiving his own soul. For he had been born in the times when Troy fought for Helen, and being the most beautiful of the sons of Panthous and the most beautifully dressed, he died so young as to give Homer occasion for a lament; and passing into several bodies according to the ordinance of Adrasteia, by which the soul changes [from body to body], he came back again into human form and was born to Mnesarchides of Samos, a sage instead of a barbarian, an Ionian instead of a Trojan, and so far undying that he had not even forgotten that he had been Euphorbus. I have told you, then, the ancestor of my wisdom, and that I did not discover these things myself, but hold them as heir of another. And I do not put on trial those who indulge themselves in the scarlet bird, or in the bird from the Phasis or from Paeonia, which those who gratify their bellies in everything fatten for their feasts; nor have I ever yet indicted anyone over the fish which the grandees buy for more than men once paid for koppa-branded horses; nor have I begrudged anyone a purple robe, or some Pamphylian or soft garment; yet I — O gods! — am defending myself against an indictment over asphodel and dried fruits and clean fare; and not even my clothing is safe from seizure, but the accuser strips me of that too, as something of great value to sorcerers. And yet, if you set aside the argument about living and lifeless things, by which a man is thought pure or not, in what way is linen better than wool? Wool was shorn from the gentlest of animals, one cherished by the gods, who do not disdain the shepherd's work, and who, by Zeus, once even deemed it worthy of a golden form — whether the gods did so or the stories. Flax is sown just anyhow, and there is no story of gold attached to it; but nevertheless, because it was not plucked from a living creature, it is thought pure by the Indians and pure by the Egyptians, and for this reason it has become the dress of Pythagoras and of me when we converse, pray, and sacrifice. It is pure, too, to spend the night under it; for to those who live as I do, dreams bring truer messages. Let us make a defence also for the hair I once had, since an indictment has been found even for squalor. Let the judge of it be not the Egyptian but the blond and well-combed youths, who have their lovers and the courtesans at whose doors they go revelling hanging upon them; and let them consider themselves fortunate and enviable for their hair and the perfume that drips from it, and me as utterly without charm, a lover of not loving. For this shall be said to them: "Wretches, do not slander the invention of the Dorians; for wearing long hair comes from the Lacedaemonians, who practised it in [the] times when they were at their most warlike; and Leonidas, king of Sparta, wore his hair long for the sake of courage, and to appear majestic to his friends and fearsome to his enemies; and that is why Sparta wears its hair long in pride of him, no less than of Lycurgus and Iphitus."
